1.meaning: A command meaning "Say!" — Allah is directing the Prophet (and, through him, every believer) to speak aloud the words of refuge that follow. It frames the whole surah as a divinely dictated prayer to be uttered.
1.grammar: A command (imperative) verb addressed to a single male: "you, say!" The base verb is qāla / yaqūlu ("to say"). In the command form the weak middle letter drops out, leaving the short, clipped qul ending in a silent consonant — the bare, urgent form of an order.

2.meaning: "I seek refuge / I take shelter" — the speaker declares that he is fleeing for protection to Allah, placing himself under His safekeeping against all harm. It is an act of seeking asylum with the Almighty.
2.grammar: A present-tense verb in the first person singular: "I seek refuge" (right now / continually). The a- prefix marks the doer as "I." The final -u ending is the ordinary present-tense (indicative) marker, signalling a plain, ongoing statement of fact rather than a command or a wish.
2.root: ع-و-ذ (ʿ-w-dh) — to seek refuge, to take shelter / protection

3.meaning: "In / with the Lord" — naming the One in whom refuge is taken. "Rabb" is more than "lord": it is the Master who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures and steadily brings His creation to completion; here, the Cherisher and Sustainer of mankind.
3.grammar: A particle bi- ("in, with, by") attached to the front of the noun rabb. The bi- here conveys taking hold of Allah for protection ("I take refuge IN the Lord"). Any noun governed by bi- must take the genitive case, which is why rabb ends in -i (rabbi); that -i ending also links it to the next word, giving "Lord OF mankind."
3.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, master, bring up

4.meaning: "Of mankind / of humankind" — the people, the whole human race. It specifies whose Lord is meant: Allah, the Lord of all human beings.
4.grammar: The definite article al- ("the") prefixed to the noun nās ("people"). Because nās begins with a "solar" letter (n), the l of the article is not pronounced; instead the noun's own initial n is doubled, so the pair is read an-nās (the doubling is shown by the shadda on the noun). The final -i is the genitive case ending: it marks this word as possessed by the previous one, giving "the Lord OF mankind."
4.root: أ-ن-س (ʼ-n-s) — humankind, people; human sociability / familiarity (nās is a contraction of unās, with the hamza dropped in common usage); some lexicographers alternatively relate it to ن-و-س, n-w-s, "to sway, move about"

1.meaning: The King, Sovereign, and absolute Master of all people — the One who owns them, rules over them, and commands them. Unlike an earthly king who merely governs subjects he does not own, Allah is King in the fullest sense: He possesses, sustains, and has complete authority over every human being.
1.grammar: A noun standing in apposition to 'Rabbi' (Lord) from the previous verse, so it shares the same role. The final -i ending is genitive (the majrūr case): here it does two jobs at once — it carries over the genitive from the preposition 'bi' (in) of verse 1 ('I seek refuge in the Lord… the King…'), and it links this word to the next as a possessive construct (it is the muḍāf), giving 'King OF…'.
1.root: م-ل-ك (m-l-k) — ownership, dominion, kingship, sovereign authority

2.meaning: Humankind — all people collectively. The word denotes human beings as a category, the very ones being urged to seek refuge. Its repetition across the surah (after 'Lord of mankind') gives the supplication its rhythm and drives home that Allah's lordship, kingship, and divinity all belong over the same humanity.

parts.en: the (definite article 'al-', its 'l' assimilated into the following 'n')

2.grammar: A definite noun: the prefix 'al-' is 'the', but its 'l' is not pronounced — it merges into the doubled 'n' of 'nās' (so 'an-nās', not 'al-nās'), 'n' being a sun letter. The final -i ending is genitive, marking it as the second part of the possessive construct (the muḍāf ilayhi): 'King OF mankind'.
2.root: أ-ن-س (a-n-s) — sociability, companionship, humanity; the mainstream derivation, where 'al-nās' is held to be a contraction of 'al-unās' (people). (A minority instead trace it to ن-و-س, n-w-s, 'to sway'.)

1.meaning: The God of mankind: the one true Deity who alone is worthy of worship, the ultimate object of every heart's adoration, fear, love, and obedience. This is the third of the three divine attributes invoked in this surah (Lord, King, God), naming Allah as the only being deserving of worship.

parts.en: god / deity (the one worthy of worship)
of (genitive ending linking to the next word)

1.grammar: A singular masculine noun in the genitive case, functioning as the possessed term (muḍāf) of a possessive construction (iḍāfa) — it continues the chain begun in the previous verses, standing in apposition to 'Lord' and 'King'. The final kasra (-i) ending is genitive: here it means 'OF', linking 'God' to the following word so it reads 'God OF mankind'. Note this is the common noun ilāh ('a god / the deity'), the same root from which the name Allah (al-ilāh, 'the God') is formed; it is not the proper name Allah itself.
1.root: أ-ل-ه (ʾ-l-h) — worship, divinity; the quality of being the one deserving of worship

2.meaning: Mankind / humanity: people in general, the whole of the human race. By repeating this word a third time (Lord of mankind, King of mankind, God of mankind), the verse drives home that Allah's lordship, sovereignty, and divinity all belong to Him over the very people who are being urged to seek His protection.
2.grammar: A definite collective noun ('the people / mankind') in the genitive case, functioning as the possessor (muḍāf ilayhi) of the preceding word. The prefix al- is 'the'; its 'l' assimilates into the following 'n' (a sun letter), which is why it is pronounced an-nās and written with a doubled n (shadda). The final kasra (-i) ending is genitive because this word is possessed by 'God' before it: 'God OF mankind'. The little mark after it (a small ـۙ) is a recitation pause sign, not part of the word.
2.root: ن-و-س (n-w-s) — to move/stir about; the sense behind nās, 'humankind, people' (the stronger majority view derives it from أ-ن-س, ʾ-n-s, relating to companionship and being human)

1.meaning: A preposition meaning 'from' or 'out of'. Here it marks the source or origin of what one is seeking refuge from — 'I seek refuge... FROM the evil of...'. It points to the thing being guarded against.
1.grammar: This is a non-inflecting preposition (it never changes its ending). It governs the noun after it and forces that noun into the genitive case — which is why the next word 'sharr' takes an -i ending (sharri). Think of it as 'from' pulling whatever follows into a 'from-the-X' relationship.

2.meaning: Evil, harm, or wickedness — that which causes injury, distress, or corruption. It is the abstract noun for badness itself, the thing from which protection is sought.
2.grammar: The final -i ending is genitive, and it is doing two jobs at once. First, it is genitive because the preposition 'min' before it requires that case ('from the evil'). Second, 'sharri' is itself the first half of a possessive pair (iḍāfa) with the next word, so the -i also links it to what follows: 'the evil OF the whisperer'. The word carries no 'the' of its own because being the first term of such a pair makes it definite through the following definite noun.

3.meaning: The whisperer — and far more than an occasional whisper. The form is an intensive one, so it names a being who is the very embodiment of whispering: one who constantly slips secret, barely-audible suggestions into the mind. It refers to the devil (Shaytan) as the source of insinuating, prompting thoughts.
3.grammar: The prefix 'al-' is 'the', and its 'l' is pronounced clearly here: waw (و) is a 'lunar' letter, so there is no assimilation — you say 'al-waswās' with an audible l. The word is built from the four-consonant (quadriliteral) root w-s-w-s, which is itself a reduplication (the pair w-s repeated). 'Waswās' is its intensive/instance noun pattern, turning the simple act of whispering into a fixed trait — 'the one who whispers and whispers'. (This is a different morphological class from word 4's faʿʿāl pattern, which works by doubling a middle consonant rather than by reduplicating a root.) The final -i ending is genitive because this word is the second half of the possessive pair begun by 'sharr': 'the evil OF the whisperer'.
3.root: و-س-و-س (w-s-w-s) — to whisper, to insinuate faint promptings

4.meaning: The one who slinks back and withdraws. Again an intensive form: it describes the whisperer's habit of retreating and shrinking away — classically understood as Shaytan drawing back the moment a person remembers Allah, only to creep forward again when the heart grows heedless.
4.grammar: The prefix 'al-' is 'the', and its 'l' is pronounced clearly: khāʾ (خ) is a 'lunar' letter, so there is no assimilation — you say 'al-khannās' with an audible l. The stem follows the intensive faʿʿāl pattern (فَعَّال), formed by doubling the middle radical (the n of the root kh-n-s), which signals a settled habit rather than a one-time act — 'the one who slinks away again and again'. The final -i ending is genitive here because it is a second adjective describing 'al-waswās' and must match that word, which was already genitive; so it simply agrees with the whisperer it modifies ('the whisperer, the slinking one').
4.root: خ-ن-س (kh-n-s) — to draw back, recede, slink away furtively

1.meaning: A relative pronoun meaning "the one who" or "who." It links back to the whisperer mentioned in the previous verse and introduces the description that follows, telling us what this being habitually does. Think of it as opening a clause: "...the [whisperer], the very one who..."
1.grammar: This is a masculine singular relative pronoun, used here for a male/singular referent (the whisperer). It is a single fused, indivisible word — not a noun carrying a detachable "al-" article. The doubled l (shown by the shadda on لّ) belongs to the pronoun itself. Its form stays alladhī whether it is subject or object (it does not inflect for case). Its job is purely to connect: it ties the noun before it to the verb-clause after it, like the English "who" in "the one who whispers."

2.meaning: Means "he whispers" — to plant a faint, secret suggestion in someone's mind; to insinuate evil thoughts so quietly that no outward voice is heard. The repeated, echoing shape of the word (was-wis) mimics the murmuring nature of whispering itself.
2.grammar: This is a present/ongoing-tense verb, third-person masculine singular: "he whispers / keeps whispering." The yu- prefix marks "he," and the final -u ending shows the verb is in its base (indicative) state, signalling a real, habitual, continuing action — this is what the whisperer constantly does. It is built on a four-consonant (quadriliteral) root, و-س-و-س, formed by repeating the two-sound unit و-س; this reduplication is what conveys the repeated, low murmuring of whispering.
2.root: و-س-و-س (w-s-w-s) — whispering, faint insinuating suggestion; a quadriliteral root formed by reduplicating the unit و-س

3.meaning: A preposition meaning "in" or "into / within." It points to the location where the whispering takes place — inside, deep within the chests of people.
3.grammar: An indeclinable preposition: its form never changes. Grammatically it puts the noun that follows it ("breasts") into the genitive case, which is why that next word carries an -i ending. It conveys containment — the thoughts are cast within the inner self.

4.meaning: Means "the chests / breasts" — and by extension the inner self: the heart, the seat of thoughts, intentions and feelings. In Qur'anic usage the "chest" (ṣadr) is where one's private thoughts and inclinations stir, so this names the very place the whisperer targets.

parts.en: of (genitive ending, linking to the next word)

4.grammar: This is the plural of ṣadr ("chest"). It carries a final -i ending for two reasons working together: it follows the preposition "in" (fī), and it is the first part of a possessive link ("chests OF…"). That -i tells you it is genitive and that the next word completes the phrase — "the chests of mankind."
4.root: ص-د-ر (ṣ-d-r) — chest, breast; the inner front of a person

5.meaning: Means "mankind / humankind, people." It refers to human beings in general — here, the people in whose innermost selves the whisperer tries to plant his suggestions.

parts.en: the (definite article; its "l" sound merges into the following n)

5.grammar: A definite collective noun, "the people / mankind." The al- ("the") is written but its "l" sound assimilates into the following n, so it is pronounced an-nās. The final -i ending is genitive: it completes the possessive phrase begun by the previous word, giving "the chests OF mankind."
5.root: أ-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — the standard root, from أَنِسَ (to be sociable/intimate); the initial hamza is dropped in an-nās. (A minority view derives it from ن-و-س, n-w-s, "to sway/move," but أ-ن-س is the dominant classical view.)

1.meaning: A preposition meaning 'from' or 'of'. Here it begins a clause that specifies the source or category of the whisperer described in the previous verses: the whispering comes 'from among' two kinds of beings. It identifies what class the tempter belongs to.
1.grammar: A preposition (a small linking word). It is normally just 'min', but here the silent ending is voiced as 'mina' (with a final -a) to ease pronunciation before the following word, which begins with the joining-hamza of 'al-'. A preposition like this puts the noun after it into the genitive case, which is why the next words carry an -i ending.

2.meaning: 'The jinn' — a class of unseen, intelligent beings created by Allah from smokeless fire, possessing free will like humans. The form here (al-jinnah) is a collective noun referring to jinn-kind as a whole. They are named as one source of the whispering against which refuge is sought.
2.grammar: A noun made definite by the prefix 'al-' ('the'). The final -i ending is the genitive case, triggered by the preposition 'min' before it ('from the jinn'). The -ah/-at ending marks it as a collective noun naming the whole category rather than one individual. (In careful pronunciation the doubled n is sounded, so it is often heard as 'jinnah'.)
2.root: ج-ن-ن (j-n-n) — to cover, conceal, hide (jinn are so named because they are hidden from sight)

3.meaning: 'And humankind' — the second source of the whispering: human beings. This shows that the tempter's evil suggestions can come not only from unseen jinn but also from people. The word an-nās is the recurring keyword of the surah, here joined to the jinn by 'and'.
3.grammar: Built from 'wa-' ('and') joined to the definite noun 'al-nās' ('the people'). Because it is linked by 'and' to the earlier genitive 'al-jinnah', it shares the same genitive case, shown by the final -i ending ('...and mankind'). In speech the 'l' of 'al-' assimilates into the 'n', so it sounds like 'an-nās'.
3.root: ن-و-س / أ-ن-س (n-w-s / ʾ-n-s) — humankind, people; relating to human sociability and movement
